facts.statement: Arambourgiania lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous, Maastrichtian

facts.statement: Paleontologist Camille Arambourg described the specimen as a new genus and species, Titanopteryx philadelphiae, in 1959.
facts.quote: After examination of the specimen by paleontologist Camille Arambourg, he described it as belonging to a new genus and species in 1959, Titanopteryx philadelphiae.

facts.statement: In 1989, paleontologist Lev Nessov renamed the genus from Titanopteryx to Arambourgiania to honor Camille Arambourg.
facts.quote: Because of this, paleontologist Lev Nessov in 1989 renamed the genus to Arambourgiania, in honor of Arambourg.

facts.statement: The holotype cervical vertebra of Arambourgiania measures between 77 and 78 cm in length.
facts.quote: Its cervical vertebrae are extremely elongated, with the holotype vertebra measuring 77-78 cm in length.

facts.statement: Initial estimates placed the wingspan of Arambourgiania between 11 and 13 meters, suggesting it was the largest known pterosaur.
facts.quote: Initial wingspan estimates ranged from 11 to 13 m, which would have made it the largest known pterosaur.

facts.statement: Recent research suggests the wingspan of Arambourgiania was between 8 and 10 meters, still ranking it among the largest known flying animals.
facts.quote: However, given the fragmentary remains, more recent research has suggested wingspans anywhere between 8 to 10 m, which would still place the genus among the largest known flying animals.

facts.statement: Arambourgiania is classified as a member of the pterosaur family Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: Arambourgiania is a member of the family Azhdarchidae, which includes some of the largest known pterosaurs.

facts.statement: The bones of Arambourgiania were extremely hollow and lightly built, featuring adaptations for soaring flight.
facts.quote: The bones of Arambourgiania are extremely hollow and lightly built with adaptations for soaring.

facts.statement: Arambourgiania inhabited Jordan during the Maastrichtian age of the Cretaceous period, approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Arambourgiania (meaning "Camille Arambourg's") is a genus of pterosaur, an extinct group of flying reptiles, that inhabited Jordan during the Maastrichtian age of the Cretaceous period, around 72 to 66 million years ago.

facts.statement: Fossils of Arambourgiania in Jordan are found in the Ruseifa Formation, which represents a deep marine environment from the Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: In Jordan, Arambourgiania fossils are known from the Ruseifa Formation which had deep marine environment that was deposited during the Maastrichtian.

facts.statement: In 1943, a railway worker discovered fossil fragments including an incomplete cervical vertebra measuring 60.96 cm during phosphate mining near Ruseifa, Jordan.
facts.quote: In 1943, during phosphate mining operations near the town of Ruseifa, Jordan, a railway worker found several fossil fragments associated with an incomplete fossilized cervical (neck) vertebra measuring 60.96 cm in length.

facts.statement: In 1954, Camille Arambourg misidentified the holotype vertebra as a wing metacarpal, leading to the 1959 naming of Titanopteryx philadelphiae.
facts.quote: In 1954, Arambourg interpreted the vertebra as the wing metacarpal of a giant pterosaur, and in 1959 named the new genus and species Titanopteryx philadelphiae.

facts.statement: In 1975, Douglas A. Lawson concluded that the holotype specimen was a cervical vertebra rather than a wing metacarpal, correcting an earlier interpretation.
facts.quote: In 1975 while studying Quetzalcoatlus, American paleontologist Douglas A. Lawson correctly concluded that the holotype was not a metacarpal but a cervical vertebra.

facts.statement: In 1995, David Martill and Eberhard Frey traveled to Jordan to locate the holotype and clarify the identity of Arambourgiania.
facts.quote: In 1995, paleontologists David Martill and Eberhard Frey traveled to Jordan in an attempt to find the vertebra and to clarify the identity of Arambourgiania.

facts.statement: In 1996, it was discovered that the holotype had been purchased by Hani N. Khoury in 1969 and donated to the University of Jordan in 1973.
facts.quote: However in 1996, after the departure of Martill and Frey to Europe, Rashdie Sadaqah, the engineer of the mine, found out that the holotype had been purchased by the geologist Hani N. Khoury in 1969, who then donated it to the University of Jordan in 1973.

facts.statement: Fossil remains from the United States and Morocco have been tentatively assigned to Arambourgiania, though this classification is not certain.
facts.quote: Additional fossil remains from the United States and Morocco have also been found, but their assignment to Arambourgiania is only tentative.

facts.statement: In 2018, David Martill and Markus Moser described fragmentary azhdarchid specimens from the Bavarian State Collection in Munich.
facts.quote: In 2018, a set of fragmentary azhdarchid specimens housed in the Bavarian State Collection for Palaeontology and Geology of Munich, Germany were described by paleontologists David Martill and Markus Moser.

facts.statement: In 1992, Lewy and colleagues described endocasts found in the Mishash Formation near Mitzpe Ramon, Israel, dating to the upper Campanian or early Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: In 1992, Lewy and colleagues described a pair of endocasts (a natural cast of the brain cavity) which had been unearthed from upper Campanian or early Maastrichtian-aged phosphates belonging to the Mishash Formation located near Mitzpe Ramon, Israel.

facts.statement: A 2014 study suggests the endocasts referred to Arambourgiania by Lewy likely belong to birds due to their 3 cm length and bird-like structure.
facts.quote: However, these endocasts have no overlap with any described fossils of Arambourgiania and, according to a 2014 study, most likely belong to birds instead on the basis of their length of around 3 cm and bird-like structure.

facts.statement: In 2018, Nicholas Longrich, David Martill, and Brian Andres tentatively identified an incomplete left ulna from the Ouled Abdoun Basin, Morocco, as Arambourgiania.
facts.quote: In 2018, paleontologists Nicholas Longrich, David Martill, and Brian Andres described an incomplete left ulna of the "Sidi Chennane azhdarchid" from the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Morocco which they tentatively identified as ?Arambourgiania.

facts.statement: In 2024, researchers reported a partial right humerus from the Ruseifa Phosphate Mines near Amman, Jordan, where the Arambourgiania holotype was found.
facts.quote: In 2024, the describers of the genus Inabtanin reported a partial right humerus of a large pterosaur in the Ruseifa Phosphate Mines, near the Jordanian capital of Amman, which was where the holotype of Arambourgiania was recovered.

facts.statement: Researchers concluded the humerus from the Ruseifa Phosphate Mines belonged to A. philadelphiae and was comparable in size and shape to Quetzalcoatlus northropi.
facts.quote: They concluded that the specimen belonged to A. philadelphiae and that it is comparable in size and shape to the humerus of the type species of Quetzalcoatlus, Q. northropi.

facts.statement: In 1999, Wendy Melton-Beeson discovered and T. Lynn Harrell Jr. collected a fragmentary azhdarchid cervical vertebra in Selmer, Tennessee.
facts.quote: In 1999, a fragmentary azhdarchid cervical vertebra (MPPM 2000.23.1) was discovered by Memphis local Wendy Melton-Beeson and collected by paleontologist T. Lynn Harrell Jr. that same year.

facts.statement: Arambourgiania was among the largest azhdarchids, comparable in size to Quetzalcoatlus, Hatzegopteryx, and possibly Cryodrakon.
facts.quote: Arambourgiania was among the largest azhdarchids, rivalled in size by Quetzalcoatlus and Hatzegopteryx (and possibly Cryodrakon).

facts.statement: The known remains of Arambourgiania consist of fragmentary bones including a partial femur, a partial radius, a partial humerus, two phalanges, and several partial cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: Arambourgiania is known from fragmentary remains, including an incomplete holotype cervical vertebrae, other partial cervical vertebrae, a partial radius and humerus, two phalanges (bones that make up the toes), and a partial femur.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, designated UJA VF1, is a very elongated cervical vertebra, likely the fifth in the series.
facts.quote: The holotype of Arambourgiania, UJA VF1, consists of a very elongated cervical vertebra, probably the fifth one in the cervical series.

facts.statement: The posterior portion of the holotype vertebra measures 44 mm in length and 55 mm in height with a nearly circular cross-section.
facts.quote: The posterior (back) portion of the vertebra is 44 mm long and 55 mm high and has a near circle-shaped cross section.

facts.statement: The cervical vertebrae of Arambourgiania contain a circular internal tube, a trait also found in other azhdarchids and dsungaripterids.
facts.quote: Arambourgiania preserves a circular, internal tube inside the cervical vertebrae, a feature observed in other azhdarchids and in dsungaripterids.

facts.statement: Arambourgiania lacks a dorsal pneumatic foramen above its neural canal, a feature that distinguishes it from relatives like Cryodrakon.
facts.quote: Arambourgiania lacks a dorsally (top) positioned pneumatic foramen above its neural canal, a trait typically present in relatives like Cryodrakon, distinguishing it from other azhdarchids.

facts.statement: A preserved fragment of the left femur measures 142 mm in total length.
facts.quote: The distal portion (part away from body) of an abraded left femur was also unearthed, with a total preserved length of 142 mm.

facts.statement: A fragment of the distal radius measures 108 mm but is extremely worn.
facts.quote: A probable distal radius fragment is 108 mm but extremely worn.

facts.statement: The humerus of Arambourgiania is estimated to be composed of 90% air by volume, indicating strong adaptation for flight.
facts.quote: This indicates a humerus composed of 90% air by volume, making it extremely well-adapted for flight.

facts.statement: Fragments of cervical vertebrae attributed to Arambourgiania have been found in Jordan and the United States.
facts.quote: Fragments of other cervical vertebrae have been unearthed in Jordan as well as in the United States, though none is as complete as the holotype.

facts.statement: The original holotype material, combined with plaster, was approximately 62 cm long but was sawed into three parts with the middle section now missing.
facts.quote: The original material combined with its plaster was about 62 cm long, but had been sawed into three parts, and the middle section is now missing.

facts.statement: Frey and Martill extrapolated the total neck length of the holotype to be about 3 meters.
facts.quote: The total neck length was extrapolated at about 3 m using the same method.

facts.statement: In the late 1990s, Frey and Martill estimated the wingspan of Arambourgiania to be between 11 and 13 meters based on a 1.18 ratio.
facts.quote: Applying that 1.18 ratio to the overall size, Frey and Martill concluded in the late 1990s that the wingspan of Arambourgiania was 11 to 13 m, larger than the estimated wingspan of Quetzalcoatlus, which measured 10 to 11 m.

facts.statement: In 2003, researchers suggested the wingspan of Arambourgiania was likely about 7 meters, though they provided no rationale for this estimate.
facts.quote: In 2003, the researchers who described the related pterosaur Phosphatodraco stated that the wingspan of Arambourgiania was more likely about 7 m, though this measurement was not given a rationale.

facts.statement: In 2010, Witton and Habib debated that a 7-meter wingspan was an underestimate while a 11 to 13-meter wingspan was an overestimate for Arambourgiania.
facts.quote: In 2010, paleontologists Mark Witton and Michael Habib argued that a 7 m wingspan is an underestimate for Arambourgiania, while a 11 to 13 m wingspan would be too much.

facts.statement: In 2022, Paul proposed a wingspan of 8 to 9 meters for Arambourgiania, suggesting it was smaller than Quetzalcoatlus northropi.
facts.quote: In his 2022 pterosaur book, Paul proposed that Arambourgiania had a wingspan of 8 to 9 m, making it smaller than Quetzalcoatlus northropi, which he kept at 10 to 11 m.

facts.statement: A 2024 study estimated the wingspan of Arambourgiania to be around 10 meters based on comparisons with the humerus of Quetzalcoatlus northropi.
facts.quote: In a 2024 study, the wingspan of Arambourgiania was estimated to be around 10 m based on a large humerus comparable in size to that of Q. northropi.

facts.statement: In 1984, Nessov assigned Arambourgiania (then known as Titanopteryx) to the subfamily Azhdarchinae.
facts.quote: Arambourgiania was assigned to a newly named subfamily called Azhdarchinae by Nessov in 1984, though it was still known as "Titanopteryx" at that time.

facts.statement: In 1986, Kevin Padian declared his family Titanopterygiidae a junior synonym of Azhdarchinae after realizing the cervical vertebrae diagnoses were identical.
facts.quote: Two years later, in 1986, Padian became aware of the existence of Azhdarchinae and declared his Titanopterygiidae to be a junior synonym of this taxon, as he believed that the diagnoses of the cervical vertebrae for both groups were identical.

facts.statement: Recent studies consistently classify Arambourgiania as a derived azhdarchid in the subfamily Quetzalcoatlinae, though its exact phylogenetic position remains disputed.
facts.quote: The classification of Arambourgiania as a derived (advanced) Azhdarchid in the subfamily Quetzalcoatlinae has been consistent in recent studies, though its exact position is disputed.

facts.statement: While multiple analyses place Quetzalcoatlus as the closest relative of Arambourgiania, other studies suggest a closer relationship with Mistralazhdarcho and Aerotitan.
facts.quote: One of its closest relatives is Quetzalcoatlus according to multiple phylogenetic analyses; these two genera are often recovered as sister taxa. However, several other studies instead favored a closer relationship between Arambourgiania and the azhdarchids Mistralazhdarcho and Aerotitan.

facts.statement: A 2021 phylogenetic analysis by Brian Andres places Arambourgiania as the sister taxon of Quetzalcoatlus.
facts.quote: The first cladogram is based on the phylogenetic analysis by American paleontologist Brian Andres in 2021, which places Arambourgiania as the sister taxon of Quetzalcoatlus.

facts.statement: A 2023 study by Rubi Pêgas and colleagues placed Arambourgiania in a trichotomy with Mistralazhdarcho and Aerotitan.
facts.quote: The second cladogram is based on the 2023 study by paleontologist Rubi Pêgas and colleagues and placed Arambourgiania in a trichotomy with Mistralazhdarcho and Aerotitan.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Arambourgiania likely did not have a piscivorous lifestyle similar to modern skim-feeders.
facts.quote: Witton and Naish noted that it is unlikely for azhdarchids to have had a piscivorous lifestyle similar to modern skim-feeders like skimmers and some terns

facts.statement: Arambourgiania lacked the specific cranial features required for a skim-feeding lifestyle.
facts.quote: Azhdarchids lacked cranial features such as sideways compressed lower jaws and the shock-absorbing adaptations required for this mode of feeding

facts.statement: A 2021 study suggests Arambourgiania might have been less terrestrial than previously thought by other researchers.
facts.quote: in a 2021 study, Labita and Martill noted that azhdarchids might have been less terrestrial than suggested by Witton and Naish

facts.statement: No azhdarchid fossils, including those of Arambourgiania, have been found in truly terrestrial strata.
facts.quote: Labita and Martill noted that no azhdarchids had been found in truly terrestrial strata

facts.statement: While historically interpreted as soarers, some authors have suggested Arambourgiania could have performed flapping flight similar to swans and geese.
facts.quote: Historically, azhdarchids have been interpreted as soarers, although some authors have suggested that their musculature allowed flapping flight like in swans and geese

facts.statement: A 2024 study suggests Arambourgiania was a soarer based on adaptations in its humerus similar to those in vultures.
facts.quote: A 2024 study by paleontologist Kierstin Rosenbach and colleagues compared the humerus of Arambourgiania to that of soaring birds and suggested that Arambourgiania itself was also a soarer

facts.statement: Arambourgiania is part of the only pterosaur group for which trackways have been confidently assigned.
facts.quote: Azhdarchids are the only group of pterosaurs to which trackways have been confidently assigned

facts.statement: Trackways show that Arambourgiania walked with its limbs held directly underneath its body.
facts.quote: One long trackway of this kind shows that azhdarchids walked with their limbs held directly underneath their body

facts.statement: Arambourgiania had a much weaker neck than Hatzegopteryx, indicated by its lithe, thin-walled vertebrae.
facts.quote: The lithe, thin-walled vertebrae of Arambourgiania indicate the neck was much weaker than that of Hatzegopteryx

facts.statement: The estimated body weight of Arambourgiania is between 180 and 250 kg.
facts.quote: estimated at 180 to 250 kg for Arambourgiania and Hatzegopteryx

facts.statement: Unlike Hatzegopteryx, which had a strongly muscled neck to support a robust head, Arambourgiania had fewer muscle attachments on its neck.
facts.quote: In order to support the robust head, the neck of Hatzegopteryx was likely strongly muscled, in contrast to that of Arambourgiania with its fewer muscle attachments

facts.statement: During the Maastrichtian, the sites where Arambourgiania fossils were found in Jordan and Morocco were covered by the Tethys Sea.
facts.quote: In Jordan and Morocco, Arambourgiania fossils come from sites that during the Maastricthian were covered by the Tethys Sea

facts.statement: Arambourgiania fossils in Jordan date to the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period, between 72 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Jordan In Jordan, Arambourgiania fossils have been unearthed from a series of phosphate mines in Ruseifa dating to the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period (72-66 Ma)

facts.statement: The phosphate deposits containing Arambourgiania fossils are interpreted as representing either a shallow or deep marine environment.
facts.quote: The phosphates in which Arambourgiania was found have been interpreted as either a shallow marine environment, or a deep marine environment

facts.statement: The genus Arambourgiania was described by Nesov et al. in 1987.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Nesov et al., 1987

facts.quote: subdivision: A. philadelphiae (Arambourg, 1959) (especie tipo)

facts.statement: The genus was renamed Arambourgiania in 1987 to honor Arambourg after it was found to be preoccupied by an insect name.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen VF 1 consists of a very elongated cervical vertebra, likely the fifth one.

facts.statement: The original fossil, which measured about 62 centimeters in length, is now broken into three parts with the middle section lost.

facts.statement: Frey and Martill estimated the total length of the vertebra to be 78 centimeters by comparing it to Quetzalcoatlus.

facts.statement: Based on the vertebra, the total neck length was extrapolated to be about three meters.

facts.statement: Later estimates of the wingspan have been more moderate, sometimes as low as seven meters.

facts.statement: In 1984, Nesov placed the species in the subfamily Azhdarchinae within the family Pteranodontidae.

facts.statement: Both previous classifications are now obsolete, as these forms are commonly assigned to the family Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: Ambos conceptos han caído en desuso dado que dichas formas ahora son comúnmente asignadas a la familia Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: The parent group of Arambourgiania is Azhdarchidae.
